cards.title: Three baskets
cards.explanation: All spending falls into three baskets: what you must pay every month, what you must pay now and then, and everyday choices. The first two are hard to change quickly. The third is where daily decisions add up.
cards.question: What share of your spending do you think goes on everyday choices?
cards.reveal: It is about 63%: €1,993 a month on everyday choices, against €811 on monthly must-pays and €342 on now-and-then costs.

facts.label: Everyday choices, share of spending
facts.basis: everyday basket divided by all spending

cards.title: Safe to spend
cards.explanation: Safe to spend is what is left for everyday choices after the money that is already spoken for: monthly must-pays, an amount set aside for now-and-then costs, and the saving you already do.
cards.question: After your must-pay costs and savings, how much do you think is left for everyday choices each week?
cards.reveal: About €480 a week (€2,079 a month). You actually spend €1,993 a month on everyday choices, so the gap is €87 a month to spare.

facts.label: Safe to spend per week
facts.basis: income minus must-pays, now-and-then costs and savings, divided by weeks in a month

facts.label: Safe to spend per month
facts.basis: income minus must-pays, now-and-then costs and savings

facts.label: Gap per month
facts.basis: safe to spend minus actual everyday spending

cards.title: Fixed price or spot price
cards.explanation: A fixed electricity contract charges the same price per kWh for the whole term, so the bill only moves with how much you use. A spot contract follows the hourly market price: cheaper on average in calm years, but a cold, windless week can multiply the bill.
cards.question: Your electricity bill moved between its lowest and highest month. By how much, do you think?
cards.reveal: Between €56 and €115, a swing of €59. With a fixed price that swing comes from your use alone; with a spot price the market adds its own swings on top.

facts.label: Swing between lowest and highest bill

cards.title: Buffer before investing
cards.explanation: A buffer is cash that covers your must-pay costs if income stops or a large bill lands. A common rule of thumb is three to six months. Without one, a surprise cost has to come from credit, which costs more than most investments earn.
cards.question: How many months of your must-pay costs do you think your balance covers today?
cards.reveal: About 3.63 months. Your must-pay costs average €1,153 a month, so a three-month buffer would be €3,459; your balance is €4,183.

facts.label: Months of must-pay costs covered
facts.basis: balance divided by average must-pay costs

cards.title: Growth on growth
cards.explanation: When returns are left invested, the next year's return is earned on a larger amount. Over long periods most of the result comes from that effect, not from the money paid in. Returns are never guaranteed and investments can lose value.
cards.question: If you put €50 a month aside for 10 years at 5% a year, you pay in €6,000. What would it have grown to in that scenario?
cards.reveal: About €7,796: €6,000 paid in plus about €1,796 of growth in this 5% scenario. This is an illustration, not a forecast and not advice.

cards.title: Loyalty rarely pays
cards.explanation: Providers usually keep their best prices for new customers. Checking the market once a year takes a few minutes, and a switch does not cut your service: the new provider handles the changeover.
cards.question: Your 3 monthly bills arrive one at a time. What do you think they add up to in a year?
cards.reveal: About €2,260 a year. A saving of even a tenth of that is €226 for one comparison.

cards.title: Pay yourself first
cards.explanation: Saving what is left at the end of the month rarely works, because little is left. Moving a fixed amount on payday, before any spending, turns saving into one decision instead of thirty.
cards.question: What share of your income do you think you set aside each month?
cards.reveal: About 8%: €294 a month out of €3,526 of income.
